quizzes.passage:
A Beach Worth Saving

When our school announced a volunteer clean-up of a beach on the Caspian coast, only a few students signed up. Most of us thought it would be a boring way to spend a Sunday. I went mainly because my best friend, Rashad, had promised to bring his camera.

What we found surprised everyone. In just three hours, thirty volunteers collected more than two hundred bags of rubbish. Plastic bottles were the most common item, but we also found fishing nets, shoes, a broken chair and thousands of tiny pieces of plastic mixed with the sand. A biologist from a local environmental group explained that these small pieces are especially dangerous, because birds and fish often mistake them for food.

Rashad's photos turned out to be the most powerful part of the day. He posted a 'before and after' picture of the beach, and within a week it had been shared hundreds of times. People we had never met wrote to ask when the next clean-up would take place.

The next event attracted almost a hundred volunteers, including several families with small children. Looking back, I realise that the beach did not change because of one Sunday. It changed because people saw what was possible and decided to act. Cleaning the beach is useful, but the real goal, the biologist reminded us, is to stop the rubbish from getting there in the first place.
quizzes.text: Why did the writer go to the clean-up?
options: because he wanted to meet a biologist
because his teacher made him go
because his friend was going to bring a camera
because he needed points for school
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «because his friend was going to bring a camera».

quizzes.passage:
How Habits Work

Why is it so easy to check your phone and so hard to start your homework? According to some researchers, the answer lies in the way habits are formed. They describe every habit as a loop made of three parts: a cue, a routine and a reward.

The cue is the signal that starts the behaviour — for example, the sound of a notification. The routine is the behaviour itself: picking up the phone and scrolling. The reward is the pleasant feeling that follows, such as seeing a funny message. When this loop is repeated many times, the brain begins to connect the cue with the reward, and the routine becomes almost automatic.

The good news is that the same loop can be used to build useful habits. Experts suggest keeping the cue simple and visible: if you want to read more, leave a book on your pillow. They also recommend starting with a very small routine, such as reading just two pages, so that it does not feel like hard work. Finally, giving yourself a small reward, like ticking a box on a calendar, helps the brain remember that the behaviour is worth repeating.

Breaking a bad habit is usually harder than starting a new one. Instead of simply trying to stop, it often works better to keep the same cue and reward but change the routine. A student who snacks when bored, for instance, might go for a short walk instead.
quizzes.text: In the phone example, what is the cue?
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «the sound of a notification».

Why is it so easy to check your phone and so hard to start your homework? According to some researchers, the answer lies in the way habits are formed. They describe every habit as a loop made of three parts: a cue, a routine and a reward.

The cue is the signal that starts the behaviour — for example, the sound of a notification. The routine is the behaviour itself: picking up the phone and scrolling. The reward is the pleasant feeling that follows, such as seeing a funny message. When this loop is repeated many times, the brain begins to connect the cue with the reward, and the routine becomes almost automatic.

The good news is that the same loop can be used to build useful habits. Experts suggest keeping the cue simple and visible: if you want to read more, leave a book on your pillow. They also recommend starting with a very small routine, such as reading just two pages, so that it does not feel like hard work. Finally, giving yourself a small reward, like ticking a box on a calendar, helps the brain remember that the behaviour is worth repeating.

Breaking a bad habit is usually harder than starting a new one. Instead of simply trying to stop, it often works better to keep the same cue and reward but change the routine. A student who snacks when bored, for instance, might go for a short walk instead.

The student has no habits at all.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Boredom is still the cue, but the routine has changed.».

quizzes.passage:
A Letter from Abroad

Dear Leyla,

It has been almost three months since I arrived in Germany for my exchange year, and I finally have time to write a proper letter. The first weeks were much harder than I expected. I had studied German for two years, but on my first day at school I understood almost nothing. Everyone spoke so fast! I went home and cried, and I seriously thought about coming back.

My host family helped me more than I can say. Every evening at dinner, my host mother asked me to describe my day in German, and she never laughed at my mistakes. My host brother, Jonas, introduced me to his friends and took me to his football club, even though I am a terrible player.

Now things are different. Last week I gave a short presentation about Azerbaijan in my geography class. I showed photos of Baku and the mountains of Quba, and my classmates asked so many questions that the teacher had to stop us. I have also learned to cook a German potato salad, although I still prefer our plov.

The most important thing I have learned is that feeling lost is normal at the beginning. If you decide to apply for the exchange programme next year, don't let the first difficult weeks scare you. Write back soon and tell me everything about school!

With love,
Sabina

options: She got lost on the way.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «She understood almost nothing.».

quizzes.passage:
The Usefulness of Forgetting

Most of us think of forgetting as a failure — the name we cannot recall, the keys we cannot find. Yet a growing number of neuroscientists argue that forgetting is not simply a weakness of the brain but one of its essential functions.

Every day we take in an enormous amount of information: faces on the bus, advertisements, the colour of a stranger's coat. If the brain stored all of it with equal strength, finding what really matters would become extremely difficult, rather like searching for one document on a desk buried under thousands of papers. By allowing unimportant details to fade, the brain keeps the useful memories easier to reach.

Forgetting may also help us adapt. Imagine that your school changes its timetable. If your memory of the old timetable stayed as strong as ever, you would keep going to the wrong classroom. Weakening the old memory makes room for the new one. Researchers have also suggested that forgetting specific details helps us form general ideas: a child who forgets the exact appearance of every dog she has met can still recognise a new animal as a dog.

This does not mean that all forgetting is healthy. Diseases such as Alzheimer's destroy memories that people need and value. The point, scientists say, is balance. A good memory is not one that keeps everything; it is one that keeps the right things.

options: Children forget more than adults do.
Forgetting is a normal and useful part of how the brain works.
Memory problems are caused by advertisements.
People should train themselves never to forget.
Forgetting is always a sign of illness.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Forgetting is a normal and useful part of how the brain works.».

quizzes.passage:
Saturdays at the Shelter

I started volunteering at the animal shelter because my school required forty hours of community service, and the shelter was the closest place to my house. I'll be honest: I expected to spend a few hours playing with puppies and then go home. On my first day, the manager handed me a pair of rubber gloves and pointed at a row of very dirty cages.

The first month was mostly cleaning, washing bowls and carrying heavy bags of food. The animals I met were not always the cute, friendly pets I had imagined. Many had been abandoned or badly treated, and some were afraid of people. A grey dog named Duman hid at the back of his cage every time I came near. The staff told me not to force him, but simply to sit nearby and read aloud for ten minutes each visit.

It felt pointless for weeks. Then one Saturday, Duman crept forward and rested his head on my shoe. I didn't move in case I frightened him, and I missed my bus home — I didn't care. Two months later, a young couple adopted him, and the manager let me be the one to put on his new collar.

I finished my forty hours long ago, but I still go every Saturday. Volunteering taught me something my school never planned to teach: that patience is not the same as waiting. Waiting is doing nothing; patience is continuing to do the right thing even when you can't see any results yet.
quizzes.text: Why did the writer first go to the shelter?
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «to complete a school requirement».

I'll be honest: I expected to spend a few hours playing with puppies and then go home. On my first day, the manager handed me a pair of rubber gloves and pointed at a row of very dirty cages.

The first month was mostly cleaning, washing bowls and carrying heavy bags of food. The animals I met were not always the cute, friendly pets I had imagined. Many had been abandoned or badly treated, and some were afraid of people. A grey dog named Duman hid at the back of his cage every time I came near. The staff told me not to force him, but simply to sit nearby and read aloud for ten minutes each visit.

It felt pointless for weeks. Then one Saturday, Duman crept forward and rested his head on my shoe. I didn't move in case I frightened him, and I missed my bus home — I didn't care. Two months later, a young couple adopted him, and the manager let me be the one to put on his new collar.

I finished my forty hours long ago, but I still go every Saturday. Volunteering taught me something my school never planned to teach: that patience is not the same as waiting. Waiting is doing nothing; patience is continuing to do the right thing even when you can't see any results yet.

options: to practise for a school exam
to stop the dog from sleeping
to teach the dog to understand words
to let the dog get used to him without pressure
to keep the other dogs quiet
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «to let the dog get used to him without pressure».

quizzes.passage:
The Real Price of a Cheap T-shirt

A T-shirt that costs less than a sandwich seems like a bargain. But economists and environmental scientists point out that the price on the label rarely reflects the real cost of making it.

The modern clothing industry, often called 'fast fashion', produces new styles every few weeks instead of every season. To keep prices low, companies make clothes in huge quantities, often in countries where wages are low and working conditions are poorly controlled. Growing cotton requires large amounts of water, while synthetic fabrics such as polyester are made from oil and release tiny plastic fibres when they are washed. These fibres eventually reach rivers and seas.

Because the clothes are cheap, people buy more of them and wear each item fewer times. Many garments are thrown away after only a handful of uses, and only a small percentage of textiles are recycled into new clothing. The rest is burned or buried.

Critics of this view argue that fast fashion has also made clothing affordable for millions of families who could not previously buy new clothes, and that the industry provides jobs in developing countries. Most experts agree, however, that consumers can reduce the damage without spending more: by buying fewer items of better quality, repairing clothes, and choosing second-hand shops. As one researcher put it, 'The most sustainable garment is the one already in your wardrobe.'

options: It does not show the full cost of producing it.
It includes the cost of recycling.
It is controlled by the government.
It is the same in every country.
It is usually higher than the real cost.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «It does not show the full cost of producing it.».

quizzes.passage:
The Hidden Network Under the Forest

Walk through a forest and you will see trees standing apart from each other, each apparently competing for light and water. Underground, however, the picture may be very different. The roots of most trees are connected to thin threads of fungi, which spread through the soil and form a vast network.

This partnership benefits both sides. The fungi are much better than roots at collecting water and minerals such as phosphorus from the soil, and they pass some of these to the tree. In return, the tree gives the fungi sugars that it produces through photosynthesis — something the fungi cannot do themselves. Scientists call this kind of relationship, in which both partners gain, mutualism.

Some researchers have gone further, suggesting that trees use the fungal network to exchange resources with one another, and that large old trees may even support young trees growing in their shade. These ideas have become very popular, and the network is sometimes described as a 'wood wide web'.

Other scientists, however, warn that the evidence for trees deliberately 'helping' each other is limited, and that popular articles often exaggerate the findings. They accept that the fungal connections exist and matter, but say much more research is needed before we can claim that forests behave like cooperative communities. The debate is a good reminder that an attractive idea is not the same as a proven one.

options: Old trees are taller than young ones.
Trees look separate above ground but are connected below it.
Forests are darker in winter than in summer.
Roots need more light than leaves.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Trees look separate above ground but are connected below it.».

Interviewer: You've worked night shifts in a hospital for twelve years. What surprised you most at the beginning?

Leyla: How different the hospital feels. In the daytime there are visitors, doctors doing their rounds, phones ringing constantly. At three in the morning it's quiet, but it isn't calm. You have fewer staff and no one to ask quickly, so every decision feels heavier.

Interviewer: How does the night shift affect your health?

Leyla: Honestly, it's the hardest part. Your body never fully gets used to sleeping during the day. I wear an eye mask, I have thick curtains, and I switch my phone to silent, but if a neighbour starts drilling at noon, my 'night' is over. I've learned to protect my sleep the way other people protect their savings.

Interviewer: Then why have you stayed for so long?

Leyla: Because of the patients. At night people are often frightened. They can't sleep, their families have gone home, and they want someone to talk to. During the day there's no time for that. At night I can sit with an elderly man for ten minutes and listen to stories about his village. For him, those ten minutes might be the best part of his stay. For me, they're the reason I do this job.

Interviewer: What advice would you give a young nurse starting nights?

Leyla: Eat proper meals, not just snacks from a machine. Don't be too proud to ask for help. And remember that the quiet hours are not empty hours.

Patients are more seriously ill at night.

quizzes.passage:
Why Some Words Survive

Languages are constantly changing. New words appear, old words disappear, and some words survive for thousands of years almost unchanged. Linguists have long wondered why some words are so resistant to change.

One answer seems to be frequency. Studies comparing related languages have found that words people use very often — such as the words for 'I', 'two', 'who' and 'night' — tend to change more slowly than rare words. The more often a word is used, the more firmly it is fixed in speakers' memories, and the less likely it is to be replaced.

This may seem surprising, because frequent words are also the ones most often shortened or pronounced carelessly. But there is a difference between changing a word's sound and replacing the word completely. A common word may be worn down in pronunciation, like a coin that loses its sharp edges from being passed from hand to hand, yet it remains the same coin.

Irregular verbs in English offer a related example. The most common verbs, such as 'be', 'go' and 'have', remain irregular, while many rare verbs that were once irregular have become regular over the centuries. 'Helped', for instance, replaced an older irregular form. Speakers simply forget unusual forms of words they rarely use, and so they follow the general rule instead.
quizzes.text: According to the text, which words tend to change most slowly?
options: words that are used very often
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «words that are used very often».

quizzes.passage:
The Debate

Nigar had been chosen to argue against school uniforms in the regional debating final, and she was not happy about it. Personally, she liked her uniform. It saved time in the morning, and she never had to worry about what to wear. 'How can I argue for something I don't believe?' she asked her coach, Mr Hasanov.

'That's exactly why debate is useful,' he replied. 'If you can understand the strongest arguments on the other side, you'll understand your own opinion better too.' He made her spend a week reading articles by people who disagreed with her. Slowly she began to see their point: some families found uniforms expensive, some students felt uniforms ignored their identity, and in some schools there was little evidence that uniforms improved behaviour.

In the final, Nigar spoke clearly and calmly. When the other team claimed that uniforms 'always' reduced bullying, she asked politely for their evidence, and they could not give a convincing answer. Her team won.

Afterwards, a journalist asked if she had changed her mind about uniforms. Nigar laughed. 'Not completely,' she said. 'I still like mine. But now I know why someone else might not — and I don't think they're wrong to feel that way.'
quizzes.text: Why was Nigar unhappy at the beginning?
options: She had to argue for a view she did not share.
She did not like her coach.
She had not been chosen for the final.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «She had to argue for a view she did not share.».

'That's exactly why debate is useful,' he replied. 'If you can understand the strongest arguments on the other side, you'll understand your own opinion better too.' He made her spend a week reading articles by people who disagreed with her. Slowly she began to see their point: some families found uniforms expensive, some students felt uniforms ignored their identity, and in some schools there was little evidence that uniforms improved behaviour.

In the final, Nigar spoke clearly and calmly. When the other team claimed that uniforms 'always' reduced bullying, she asked politely for their evidence, and they could not give a convincing answer. Her team won.

Afterwards, a journalist asked if she had changed her mind about uniforms. Nigar laughed. 'Not completely,' she said. 'I still like mine. But now I know why someone else might not — and I don't think they're wrong to feel that way.'

options: She asked the judges to stop the debate.
She politely asked them for evidence.
She told them they were lying.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «She politely asked them for evidence.».
